transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-02-20 14:30 UTC | Duration: ~62m | Attendees: Jesse Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Oliver Park (Hydra CTO), Rina Chen (Hydra SRE), Samir Patel (Hydra ML)

Summary: Deep technical session focused on Hydra Labs' p95/p99 tail latency pain points. Covered streaming vs non-streaming paths, KV/prefix cache behavior, batching tradeoffs, quantization impacts, network hops for VPC/on-prem, and mitigation strategies (warm pools, prioritized queues, fallbacks). Agreed next steps: Redwood to run targeted benchmarks and share logs/security docs; Hydra to provide representative payloads and schedule on-prem POC.

Topics: p95/p99 breakdown, cold vs hot KV cache misses, batching window sizing, continuous batching, int8/int4 quant tradeoffs for latency & quality, streaming protocols and chunk sizing, TLS & VPC network hops, dedicated pools & autoscale, trace artifacts to gather.

[00:00] Jesse: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm jesse from redwood, maya's our systems engineer, we'll dive straight into the tail latency stuff.
[00:10] Oliver: yep thanks, i'm oliver. context — Hydra runs a multi-tenant inference layer for our doc summarization product, seeing p95 around 120ms but p99 spikes to 800-1,200ms during peak. our SLA target is p99 < 250ms.
[00:25] Maya: okay that's a big gap. can you give us typical request size, avg tokens, streaming or non-streaming?
[00:33] Rina: mostly streaming websocket for live transcripts, average prompt ~120 tokens, completion targets ~350 tokens, so longer contexts, lots of concurrent small requests during peak.
[00:45] Samir: also we run a mix of dedicated instances and some requests routed to hosted for overflow. request mix shifts during day so cache warmness is inconsistent.
[01:00] Jesse: perfect. let's start with an initial hypothesis: large p99s often come from cold KV cache misses, batching timeouts, or networking (TLS handshakes, VPC hops). we'll break it down into client -> edge -> model runtime steps.
[01:15] Maya: right. on the runtime side we look at three contributors: pure model latency (kernel & attention compute), KV cache behavior (cache hits are cheap; misses mean re-compute or larger footprint), and scheduling/queueing (batch windows and preemption). network-side we've seen TLS setup, ALB buffering, and sometimes cross-AZ hops add variability.
[01:35] Oliver: we suspect streaming adds overhead. streaming seems to perform worse p99 than non-streaming in our tests. any common causes?
[01:45] Maya: yes streaming vs non-streaming differs mainly in 1) extra serialization/deserialization on server and client for each chunk, 2) smaller per-chunk batching which increases scheduling pressure, and 3) backpressure handling with websockets can create head-of-line queues. if streams are unbatched small-chunk requests you get more jitter.
[02:05] Samir: so is it better to use non-streaming for consistent tail latency?
[02:10] Maya: often non-streaming gives more consistent p99 because you let the runtime batch the whole token generation; but you lose user-perceived latency improvements that streaming gives for first token. it's a tradeoff. for Hydra's SLAs maybe hybrid: streaming first token, then coalesce subsequent tokens into batched frames.
[02:30] Rina: what about KV cache cold starts? we saw p99 blow up when a model variant gets a cache miss.
[02:36] Maya: KV cache misses are large contributors. when the KV is cold, the runtime has to do more attention work and can't reuse past key/value states. mitigation: prefix caching, proactive warming (replay top N prefixes), or sticky routing to keep sessions on warm workers. also dedicated pools with warm caches help.
[02:55] Jesse: another leaky factor is serialization overhead in the VPC path — for private deployments, TLS termination, proxies, and sidecars can create extra hops. Rina, do you terminate TLS at your ingress or pass-through?
[03:10] Rina: we terminate at our LB and then do mTLS to backends, so there are two TLS terminations. some requests hit a service mesh for observability which adds latency.
[03:20] Maya: each TLS hop adds a variable delay. also if keepalives are misconfigured you get more frequent handshakes. check TCP keepalive and connection reuse. for websockets, ensure the LB supports sticky connections and that idle timeouts don't close sockets.
[03:35] Oliver: on quantization, we've tested int8 and saw minor quality delta but big speedups for throughput. p99 didn't improve as much as p95 though. why?
[03:45] Maya: quant helps raw compute time but tail is often dominated by non-compute events (scheduling, cache misses, networking). if quant reduces per-token time by 20% but you still have occasional cache misses or long serialization, p99 won't proportionally drop. however quant reduces variance when compute is the dominant factor. also certain kernels for int4/int8 can introduce extra memory copies if not in-place which hurts tail.
[04:10] Samir: interesting. we also run some models with kv-cache-on-disk fallback to save memory — could that be causing spikes?
[04:18] Maya: yes paging KV to disk is a huge source of p99 spikes. any disk I/O for active KV is a no-go for strict tail SLOs. if you must oversubscribe memory, consider LRU eviction thresholds and keep hot prefixes pinned to RAM or run a dedicated pool where KV lives.
[04:35] Jesse: let's talk batching windows. Hydra currently uses a fixed 8ms batching window in the ingress. we see high p95 but p99 jumps. is that small window causing issues?
[04:45] Maya: small windows reduce added batching latency but can limit batch sizes so GPU kernel efficiency drops; conversely large windows help throughput but increase p95. tail behavior comes from variable queueing: when traffic surges, some requests wait for the batch to fill and then see longer waits plus compute. adaptive batching that caps the window but increases batch size when underutilized can help. also prioritized queues for low-latency routes (high-priority customer queries) are valuable.
[05:15] Rina: what about pre-emption with GPUs? we've seen stray requests get preempted and wait for a long time.
[05:20] Maya: preemption (eviction of running inference for higher priority) can spike tail. Redwood's runtime supports priority lanes and soft preemption; we also use fast context switching only for small models. for large models you want dedicated workers or pre-warmed preempt-resilient lanes.
[05:40] Oliver: network hops — do cross-AZ calls matter that much?
[05:45] Maya: yes, a cross-AZ hop might add 5-10ms average but with variance; if you have two hops you amplify that. For p99 even small added jitter compounds. Keep model runtime and fronting proxies in same AZ, use local egress, and minimize sidecar hops.
[06:05] Samir: any recommended traces/logs for root cause analysis? we can provide our logs but what should you prioritize?
[06:12] Maya: prioritized artifacts: 1) per-request timing breakdown (client->ingress, ingress queue wait, batch wait, kernel compute time, kv hit/miss flag, network hop times), 2) system-level metrics (CPU steal, GPU utilization, memory pressure), 3) sampling of raw payloads and sizes, 4) socket-level metrics (TLS handshake counts, connection reuse), 5) flamegraphs from the runtime and any sidecar. if you can provide p99/p95 by route and per-model, that's ideal.
[06:40] Jesse: we'll run an experiment: steady-state 1k rps with representative payloads, measure streaming vs non-streaming, and collect per-request traces. we'll share the scripts and an aggregated CSV.
[06:52] Rina: about streaming chunk sizes — we see small chunk sizes (<=64 tokens) more jitter. larger chunk sizes help?
[06:58] Maya: yes bigger chunks amortize overhead and increase batchability. The first-token latency benefit of streaming is still achievable by sending a small first chunk then coalescing. also use chunk-level batching on the server: buffer small chunks for up to X ms to batch with other clients.
[07:18] Oliver: what about fallback models? we sometimes route to a smaller faster variant under load; does that help p99?
[07:24] Maya: fallback to smaller variants reduces absolute latency and often tightens p99, but you need output-quality safeguards. Redwood supports automatic fallback policies by cost/latency tiers with quality gates and A/B monitoring. For tail SLOs, fallback is effective as long as you detect degraded worker performance quickly and failover fast.
[07:42] Samir: are there any kernel-level optimizations we should be aware of? we use mixed precision but aren't sure about fused attention kernels.
[07:50] Maya: fused attention kernels and layout-optimized ops can improve both mean and tail if they reduce memory copies and synchronization points. kernel queuing and per-thread affinity tuning reduce jitter from OS scheduling. also ensure pinned memory and avoid host-device copies in hot paths.
[08:08] Rina: we plan a private deployment (VPC) next quarter. what VPC-specific impacts on p99 should we expect?
[08:15] Maya: private deployments can reduce noisy neighbor variance but introduce operator-managed network components (firewalls, proxies). If you run in your VPC, you control placement to keep AZ locality; but misconfigured NAT gateways or transit gateways can cause asymmetric routes. Also consider KMS latencies for per-request encryption operations. Key fetches shouldn't be on the hot path.
[08:35] Oliver: any quick wins we can do in the next week?
[08:38] Maya: yes: 1) Ensure long-lived connections and tune keepalive, 2) increase sticky session timeouts for websockets, 3) pin hot prefixes for top 10 routes, 4) reduce frequency of KV eviction during peak, 5) implement a fast-path for first-token streaming, 6) sample and share p99 traces to us.
[09:00] Jesse: let's get more concrete on the benchmark we'll run. we'll need your representative payloads and a list of priority routes. we'll run 3 experiments: baseline (your current infra), dedicated warm pool (simulate pinned KV), and streaming-coalesced. we'll capture p50/p95/p99 and full timing breakdowns.
[09:18] Samir: ok we'll provide payloads. how do you capture kernel-level timings?
[09:22] Maya: the runtime emits kernel compute timings and batch histograms. we'll also enable high-res epoch timers and optionally eBPF captures to correlate syscalls/blocking. this will add minor overhead (~1-2%).
[09:36] Rina: any caveats on measuring streaming vs non-streaming fairly?
[09:40] Maya: ensure identical prompts and token budgets, measure both first-token latency and end-to-end. for streaming, instrument chunk timing and include client-side buffering behavior. also disable client-side artificial throttles.
[09:55] Oliver: our current autoscale threshold is CPU-based; should we move to queue-length or GPU util?
[10:00] Maya: queue-length or observed queue wait time is better for latency SLOs. GPU util reacts slower. You can hybridize: scale on queue length short-term and on GPU util for long-term. Also pre-warm capacity before anticipated spikes.
[10:20] Jesse: talk about prioritization -- will segregating low-latency customers into dedicated lanes help?
[10:25] Maya: absolutely. Dedicated lanes with reserved slots and strict preemption policies ensure predictable p99. requires capacity commit but for key customers it's worth it.
[10:35] Samir: we have a weird pattern: p99 spikes correlate with GC events in sidecar process. could GC cause that level of tail?
[10:41] Maya: yes, GC or stop-the-world events in any component on the request path can dominate p99. minimize GC by tuning heap, use non-blocking collectors, or move heavy serialization to native code paths. sample flamegraphs to confirm.
[10:58] Rina: any differences between gRPC and HTTP streaming for tail behavior?
[11:02] Maya: gRPC (HTTP/2) supports multiplexing over one connection which helps keep connection counts down but head-of-line blocking in HTTP/2 can surface. HTTP/1.1 chunked responses with independent connections avoid some H2 serialization but cost more connections. For websockets you get long-lived pipes but need sticky routing. Choose based on your topology; test both.
[11:25] Oliver: what instrumentation artifacts do you need that we might not have?
[11:29] Maya: per-request tracing with timing spans (ingress, batch enqueue, batch window, kernel start/end, kv hit flag), socket reuse stats, and aggregated batch histograms. If you can provide a p99-oriented heatmap (time-of-day vs p99) that's helpful.
[11:50] Jesse: we'll also look at model-variant rollouts. small changes in tokenization or prompt length can dramatically affect p99. do you keep prompt normalization?
[11:59] Samir: yes we apply some normalization but there are edge cases.
[12:03] Maya: normalize to reduce variance; pad/truncate consistently to avoid wide token length distribution which leads to batching variance.
[12:18] Rina: any suggestions on KB for warmup sizes? we have limited memory.
[12:22] Maya: track hot prefixes and warm the top X% that cover 90% of traffic. If memory limited, warm aggressively for priority customers only. Also consider compressed KV encodings or quantized KV to save RAM at the cost of some CPU.
[12:40] Oliver: one more on hardware: is moving to faster interconnects (NVLink) helping tail?
[12:45] Maya: yes NVLink/GPUDirect reduce host-device copies and lower inter-GPU sync jitter. For multi-GPU models, network fabric latency variance shows up in tail. Using colocated GPU pools with fast fabric reduces p99.
[13:00] Samir: when you run the bench, what will you share? raw timelines, batch histograms, and guidance?
[13:05] Jesse: we'll share a zip with raw CSV traces, an analysis notebook with p50/p95/p99 breakdowns, and recommended config diffs we tried.
[13:12] Rina: are there any Redwood runtime knobs we can tweak that are low-risk?
[13:16] Maya: yes: 1) enable prefix caching for top routes, 2) reduce eviction aggressiveness, 3) enable prioritized lanes for low-latency traffic, 4) use hybrid batching (fast first-token path + larger subsequent batches). We'll supply recommended values.
[13:32] Oliver: ok sounds good. recap and next steps?
[13:35] Jesse: recap: Redwood to run 3 benchmarks (baseline, warmed dedicated pool, streaming-coalesced) against representative payloads; collect per-request traces and batch histograms; share SOC2/security docs and pricing; Hydra to provide payloads and p99 traces and to confirm POC schedule.
[13:52] Samir: i'll get the payloads and a list of top routes today.
[13:55] Rina: i'll check keepalive and sticky session config and share LB topology.
[13:58] Jesse: i'll email the benchmark harness and request template, maya will run the bench and share logs, we'll reconvene after initial results. thanks all.
[14:05] Oliver: thanks everyone.
